title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions

paper.title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
paper.abstract: Abstract We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand r r , the goal is to estimate Z = ∫ 𝒟 r ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x Z=\int_{\mathcal{D}}r(x)\,\mathrm{d}x on 𝒟 ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} . Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} and do not respect the domain constraint x ∈ 𝒟 x\in\mathcal{D} . We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of Z Z . For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating r r . We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: We consider the problem of estimating high-dimensional integrals over bounded constrained domains. Let 𝒟 ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded convex domain, and let r : 𝒟 → ℝ ≥ 0 r:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be measurable and satisfy ∫ 𝒟 r ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x < ∞ \int_{\mathcal{D}}r(x)\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty . Our goal is to estimate the integral Z = ∫ 𝒟 r ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x . Z=\int_{\mathcal{D}}r(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. (1) Integrals of this form are a computational bottleneck across the sciences. In statistical physics and chemistry, free energies and thermodynamic observables are logarithms of such constants, and learned samplers have been used to estimate them for many-body systems and lattice field theories ( Noé et al., 2019 ; Wirnsberger et al., 2020 ; Nicoli et al., 2021 ) . In computer graphics, every pixel of a rendered image is an integral over light paths, parameterized so that the integration domain is the unit cube ( Müller et al., 2019 ) . In computational finance, the price of a path-dependent derivative is an expectation over a discretized asset path, which the standard inverse-CDF construction turns into an integral over [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} with d d the number of monitoring dates ( Glasserman, 2004 ; Dick et al., 2013 ) . In Bayesian statistics, the model evidence is an integral of an unnormalized posterior ( Kloek & Van Dijk, 1978 ; Kass & Raftery, 1995 ) , confined to a bounded region whenever the parameters are subject to simplex constraints or under compactly supported priors. These tasks give rise to integration problems on bounded domains, where the location of integrand mass is unknown in advance. This motivates samplers that respect the domain constraints and adapt to where the mass lies, including when it concentrates near faces or corners, or when the integrand vanishes on parts of the domain. Existing estimators differ in how much they adapt to r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) . Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo ( Niederreiter, 1992 ; Dick et al., 2013 , QMC) spreads a deterministic point set over the cube without reference to the integrand. Bayesian quadrature ( O’Hagan, 1991 ; Rasmussen & Ghahramani, 2003 ) adapts by placing a Gaussian process prior on r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) , but at a cost cubic in the number of evaluations ( Briol et al., 2019 ) . Importance sampling relies on a proposal distribution whose choice determines the estimator’s variance ( Hammersley & Handscomb, 1964 ) . Neural proposals learn that proposal from evaluations of r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) alone, either with normalizing flows ( Rezende & Mohamed, 2015 ; Müller et al., 2019 ) or with diffusion samplers ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Berner et al., 2024 ) . The latter avoids the invertibility constraints that limit flow architectures ( Kong & Chaudhuri, 2020 ) . Diffusion samplers, however, are formulated on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} with a Gaussian reference process throughout the existing work and do not respect the constraint x ∈ 𝒟 x\in\mathcal{D} . A more thorough discussion of prior work on numerical integration methods is presented in Appendix A . To design a learnable diffusion-based proposal that respects the domain constraint, we draw inspiration from diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ) for constrained generative modeling. Existing approaches fall into two groups. The first changes the geometry in which the process evolves: mirror diffusion models map 𝒟 \mathcal{D} onto ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} through the gradient of a strictly convex potential and run a standard diffusion in the resulting dual space ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , while log-barrier diffusions equip the interior of 𝒟 \mathcal{D} with the Riemannian metric induced by the Hessian of a barrier function, under which the process remains in the interior ( Fishman et al., 2023 ) . The second group keeps the Euclidean geometry of 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and confines trajectories by reflecting them at the boundary, using reflected Brownian motion as the noising process ( Fishman et al., 2023 ; Lou & Ermon, 2023 ) . In this work, we follow the second route and adapt reflected diffusions from generative modeling to sampling, where no samples from π \pi are available and the reverse dynamics must be learned from evaluations of r r alone. We outline our contributions as follows: • We propose reflected diffusion samplers (RDS) for integration on bounded domains, extending control-based diffusion samplers ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Berner et al., 2026 ) to constrained 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Our construction uses reflected Brownian motion with a time-dependent noise schedule. When initialized from the uniform distribution ν \nu on 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , this process preserves uniform marginals ( Loper, 2020 ) and defines a tractable reference path measure for the integral ( 1 ). Girsanov’s theorem ( Le Gall, 2016 ) then transfers this representation to equivalent controlled reflected diffusions through path-space importance weights. We show that the unique zero-variance ideal proposal corresponds to the same reflected noising dynamics initialized from the normalized target π ⁡ ( x ) = r ⁡ ( x ) / Z \pi(x)=r(x)/Z , and propose to learn its reversal with a neural network-parameterized drift. The learned reversal by construction also acts as the sampler from π \pi . • We design a training objective for the learned reversal to be the KL divergence to the ideal proposal. For smooth targets, its gradients can be computed via the reparameterization trick. It includes a running control cost with a terminal potential and no boundary term, closely resembling the optimal control objective of Zhang & Chen (2022) . We also derive a REINFORCE gradient estimator with a leave-one-out baseline, which uses only the pre-reflection Gaussian transition densities and does not require gradients of r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) , applying to targets that are non-smooth or vanish to zero on part of 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , where reparameterization gradients are uninformative. Integrands that vanish on part of the domain are handled by adding a positive offset and correcting the resulting integral estimate. • We provide rigorous theoretical derivation of all components of the proposed methodology, adapting existing theoretical results to the considered setting of the variance exploding reflected diffusion samplers. In addition, we prove a total-variation accuracy bound for the designed estimator, which is a reflected version of the bound presented in Guo et al. (2026) for diffusion samplers in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . • We evaluate on Genz integrands ( Genz, 1984 ) , bounded synthetic targets, Feynman parameter integral ( Bonciani et al., 2016 ) and Asian option pricing ( L’Ecuyer, 2009 ) against Quasi-Monte Carlo, Bayesian quadrature and normalizing flow importance sampling baselines. The experiments demonstrate strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the estimate. In addition, we compare against Path Integral Sampler (PIS, Zhang & Chen (2022) ) proposal by mapping 𝒟 \mathcal{D} onto ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , and demonstrate that the learned RDS proposal achieves lower integration errors against its unconstrained counterpart. 4 Experiments
sections.text: Benchmarks . We evaluate our method on bounded-domain integration problems defined on the unit hypercube 𝒟 ¯ = [ 0 , 1 ] d \overline{\mathcal{D}}=[0,1]^{d} , using the same reflection operator as in Lou & Ermon (2023) . We consider Genz Continuous and Gaussian Peak to test smooth and non-smooth interior concentration, Genz Product Peak for sharply localized factorized structure, Genz Corner Peak for mass concentrated at a boundary corner, and Genz Discontinuous for discontinuous support with a zero-valued region ( Genz, 1984 ; Kaarnioja, 2025 ) . GMM Cube tests multimodal exploration, Stripe Cube tests concentration near boundary faces, and Funnel Cube tests adaptation to strongly varying conditional scales. Finally, we consider two real world integrals - Elliptic Two-Loop and Asian option. The Elliptic Two-Loop integral is a finite five-dimensional Feynman parameter integral over the unit cube ( Bonciani et al., 2016 ; Borowka et al., 2018 ) . And the Asian option benchmark ( L’Ecuyer, 2009 ) provides a high-dimensional problem with strong coordinate dependence, a non-smooth payoff, and a large zero-valued region. We additionally compare against PIS on the benchmark from sampling literature, namely Digits ( Blessing et al., 2024 ) , in Section 4.3 . Complete definitions and parameter settings are given in Appendix F.1 . Figure 1 : Mean absolute error as a function of dimension on Genz test integrals for the number of samples N = 2 20 N=2^{20} . Error bars show variability across independent evaluation runs. Figure 2 : Mean absolute error as a function of the number of samples used for estimation on representative benchmarks. Results for FFBQ are missing on some plots due to memory limitations of this algorithm in large dimensions. Baselines . We compare the reparameterization and reinforced variants of our method, denoted RDS-RP and RDS-RF, respectively, against Path Integral Sampler ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 , PIS) , Quasi-Monte Carlo ( Niederreiter, 1992 ; Dick et al., 2013 ) , Fast Fourier Bayesian Quadrature ( Warren & Ramos, 2024 , FFBQ) , and the normalizing flow importance sampling library ZüNIS ( Deutschmann & Götz, 2024 ) . For PIS, we map z ∈ ℝ d z\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d x\in[0,1]^{d} with the sigmoid transformation x = σ ⁡ ( z ) x=\sigma(z) and train on the change-of-variables target r ~ ​ ( z ) = r ⁡ ( σ ⁡ ( z ) ) ​ | det J σ ​ ( z ) | \widetilde{r}(z)=r(\sigma(z))\left|\det J_{\sigma}(z)\right| , which preserves the original integral. We report the absolute normalizing-constant error Δ ​ Z = | Z ^ − Z | \Delta Z=|\widehat{Z}-Z| , and show mean and standard deviation across independent evaluation runs. Full experimental details are in Appendix F.2 . Overall, RDS performs well across a broad range of targets with substantially different geometry. In particular, it remains competitive on smooth, multimodal, boundary-concentrated, and high-dimensional problems, indicating that the learned proposal is not specialized to a particular class of integrands. The strong performance across both the dimension and target-evaluation sweeps also shows that the method can effectively adapt its sampling distribution to the regions that contribute most to the integral. Figure 1 illustrates the dependence of the estimation error on dimension, while Figure 2 compares methods at matched sample budgets. The full results are given in Appendix F.3 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Problems with smooth target functions
sections.text: RDS-RP is closely related to PIS, as both optimize a diffusion proposal using pathwise reparameterization gradients. The main difference is that RDS-RP evolves directly on the constrained domain and handles the boundary by reflection. This is particularly helpful for targets such as Genz Corner Peak and Stripe Cube, where a substantial amount of mass may lie close to the boundary. In PIS, the transformation to an unconstrained space sends such points far into the tails, which makes these regions harder to represent accurately. This is consistent with the stronger performance of RDS-RP on boundary-concentrated benchmarks. Besides normalizing-constant estimation, we inspect samples generated by the learned reverse process. Figure 8 shows representative RDS samples for several cube-supported targets. These visualizations provide a complementary check that the learned dynamics capture the geometry of the target rather than only producing accurate estimates of Z Z .

When the target is locally constant, ∇ x ​ log ​ r ​ ( x ) \nabla_{x}\log r(x) provides no information about how probability mass should be moved, while at the boundary of such regions the derivative may be undefined. On these problems, RDS-RF consistently outperforms the reparameterized RDS-RP variant, demonstrating the advantage of differentiating the trajectory distribution rather than the terminal target itself. The samples for Genz Discontinuous in Figure 3 illustrate this behavior particularly clearly. RDS-RF successfully concentrates probability mass inside the non-zero-valued region and recovers the sharp support geometry despite the absence of informative local gradients outside it. This improved adaptation also translates into more accurate estimates of Z Z on both benchmarks.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented reflected diffusion samplers for integration over bounded domains. The construction replaces the Gaussian reference process of existing diffusion samplers with a reflected variance-exploding process that leaves the uniform distribution on 𝒟 \mathcal{D} invariant, where trajectories never leave the domain, and a Girsanov change of measure for reflected diffusions supplies both the training objective and the importance weights used to estimate Z Z . Across a number of benchmarks, in our experiments the developed approach supplies accurate estimates of the integral. While the proposed approach is currently limited to non-negative targets, one can consider a decomposition ∫ 𝒟 r ⁡ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x = ∫ 𝒟 r + ​ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x − ∫ 𝒟 r − ​ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x \int_{\mathcal{D}}r(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{\mathcal{D}}r^{+}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x-\int_{\mathcal{D}}r^{-}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x , then estimate both parts as discussed in Section 4.2 . We leave the analysis and evaluation of this adaptation for future work.

sections.text: Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) approximates ( 1 ) using low-discrepancy point sets: Z ^ N = N − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 N r ⁡ ( x i ) \widehat{Z}_{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r(x_{i}) . Unlike independent Monte Carlo samples, QMC points are constructed to cover [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} more uniformly, typically using digital nets or lattice rules ( Niederreiter, 1992 ; Dick et al., 2013 ) . For integrands satisfying suitable regularity conditions, QMC can achieve faster convergence than ordinary Monte Carlo. Randomized QMC methods, such as scrambled Sobol sequences, retain low-discrepancy properties while allowing randomized error estimation ( Owen, 1997 ) . However, conventional QMC point sets are constructed independently of the integrand and do not adapt to the location of its mass. Bayesian quadrature (BQ) models the integrand using a Gaussian process and conditions on its evaluations at selected points ( O’Hagan, 1991 ; Rasmussen & Ghahramani, 2003 ) . Since integration is a linear functional, the Gaussian process posterior induces a Gaussian posterior over the integral, providing both an estimate and a measure of uncertainty. Evaluation points can also be selected adaptively to reduce the posterior uncertainty ( Gunter et al., 2014 ) . For fixed kernel hyperparameters, the posterior variance depends on the evaluation locations rather than the observed function values. Consequently, its uncertainty estimates depend on the adequacy of the chosen prior ( Briol et al., 2019 ) . Standard GP-based BQ requires O ⁡ ( n 3 ) O(n^{3}) computation for n n observations, although scalable variants, including Fast Fourier Bayesian Quadrature, reduce this cost ( Warren & Ramos, 2024 ) . Its variance satisfies Var q ( Z ^ N ) = Z 2 N χ 2 ( π ∥ q ) , \operatorname{Var}_{q}(\widehat{Z}_{N})=\frac{Z^{2}}{N}\chi^{2}(\pi\|q), (28) where π = r / Z \pi=r/Z and χ 2 \chi^{2} denotes the chi-square divergence. The optimal proposal is q = π q=\pi , which gives zero variance ( Hammersley & Handscomb, 1964 ) . Since sampling directly from π \pi is generally intractable, the effectiveness of IS depends on constructing a proposal that accurately represents the regions where the target concentrates. Normalizing flows (NF) provide adaptive proposal densities through invertible transformations with tractable Jacobian determinants ( Dinh et al., 2014 ; Rezende & Mohamed, 2015 ) . For sampling from unnormalized targets, Midgley et al. (2023) combine normalizing flows with annealed importance sampling to improve the coverage of poorly represented regions. For numerical integration, Müller et al. (2019) train a flow directly from evaluations of the unnormalized integrand, without requiring samples from the normalized target. They derive importance-weighted gradients for minimizing KL ( π ∥ q θ ) \mathrm{KL}(\pi\|q_{\theta}) and also consider the chi-square divergence, which directly controls the IS variance. Their method is applied to light-transport integration and path guiding. Normalizing flows have also been applied to sampling equilibrium distributions and estimating free-energy differences in molecular systems ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . Building on neural importance sampling, Deutschmann & Götz (2024) introduce ZüNIS, a flow-based importance-sampling library for high-energy physics simulations. Normalizing flows require invertible architectures with tractable Jacobians, which restricts the available transformations; expressivity limitations for particular flow architectures have been studied by Kong & Chaudhuri (2020) . Diffusion samplers ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ; Vargas et al., 2023 ; Berner et al., 2024 ; Sendera et al., 2024 ; Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024 ; Havens et al., 2025 ) learn stochastic dynamics for sampling from unnormalized target distributions without requiring invertible neural architectures. Unlike conventional diffusion models ( Song et al., 2021 ) , which learn from samples of the target distribution, diffusion samplers are trained using its unnormalized density. The Path Integral Sampler (PIS) ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ) formulates sampling as a stochastic optimal control problem, where a reference diffusion is reweighted by a terminal potential determined by the target. Its training objective combines a quadratic control cost with a terminal density term, obtained through Girsanov’s theorem. Denoising Diffusion Samplers (DDS) ( Vargas et al., 2023 ) instead formulate sampling through the time reversal of a diffusion that transforms the target towards a tractable reference distribution. Both approaches lead to related path-space optimization objectives. The resulting path measures also permit normalizing-constant estimation through importance sampling ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Most of these sampling methods are formulated using diffusions on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} and do not directly enforce bounded-domain constraints. Reflected diffusions have previously been used for constrained generative modeling ( Lou & Ermon, 2023 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ) , while mirror diffusion models ( Liu et al., 2023 ) handle constraints through transformations to an unconstrained dual space. In contrast to these data-driven generative models, our method learns a reflected diffusion proposal from an unnormalized target, without requiring target samples. It operates directly on the bounded integration domain and handles zero-valued regions by adding a positive offset to the integrand and correcting the final estimate.

sections.heading: Appendix C Existence and reversal of the reflected laws
sections.text: The arguments in this section separate two tasks. First, the reflected-SDE and Skorokhod results of Pilipenko (2014, Theorems 2.5.1–2.5.3) and the Yamada–Watanabe discussion preceding Pilipenko (2014, Theorem 2.5.4) provide well-posedness for equations with prescribed coefficients. The required domain hypotheses are verified in Lemma C.1.1 . Second, well-posedness of an equation with a prescribed score drift does not by itself identify that equation with the reversal of the forward law. We first define the ideal reverse law by reversing the already constructed target-started forward process. The time-homogeneous reflected-reversal statement of Holk et al. (2026, Section 2, equation (4)) , followed by the local clock calculation in Lemma C.4.1 , identifies this particular reversal as a weak solution of the scheduled score SDE on [ 0 , 1 ) [0,1) . Appendix D Girsanov change of drift for reflected diffusions
sections.text: This section proves the path-law change of measure used in Theorem E.2.1 . We first apply ordinary Girsanov theory on a filtered probability space carrying a reflected solution. We then show that the resulting density depends only on the observed path, so it descends to a Radon–Nikodym derivative between coordinate path laws. The second step is where reflection requires additional work. Theorem D.1.5 combines the two steps, after which we specialize it to the learned and reference diffusions.

sections.heading: E.5 Constructing unbiased estimate after discretization
Genz integrals.
sections.text: The Genz family provides a standard collection of numerical integration test functions, used in literature ( Ott et al., 2023 ; Warren & Ramos, 2024 ) , designed to exhibit distinct forms of difficulty. We consider five out of six Genz integrals - we exclude the periodic integrand as it takes negative values, which does not fit our study. All Genz targets used here admit closed-form normalization constants Kaarnioja (2025) , which allows to produce an exact reference value for any integration result. The five Genz targets span substantially different forms of concentration. Continuous and Gaussian Peak provide smooth interior modes, Product Peak has a factorized rational structure, Corner Peak concentrates mass at a boundary corner and Discontinuous combines a hard support constraint with an exponential trend within the support. The dimensional sweep from 5 5 to 30 30 further tests whether the sampler can preserve accurate mass allocation as the number of coordinates increases. For the Genz experiments, several dimensions are considered, which are specified in the description of the corresponding problem. The concentration parameters are varied with dimension in order to prevent the benchmark from becoming either nearly uniform or excessively degenerate as d d increases. Unless otherwise stated, scalar parameters are shared across dimensions, so that the resulting target is symmetric with respect to coordinate permutations.

sections.heading: Continuous Genz.
sections.text: The Continuous Genz target is defined by r ( x ) = exp ( − ∑ k = 1 d a k | x k − u k | ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d . r(x)=\exp\left(-\sum_{k=1}^{d}a_{k}|x_{k}-u_{k}|\right),\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}. The parameter u k u_{k} specifies the location of the peak along dimension k k , while a k a_{k} controls its concentration. For all coordinates we take u k = 0.55 u_{k}=0.55 and the scalar concentration parameter is chosen as a k = a ∈ { 8.0 , 5.0 , 4.0 , 3.0 } a_{k}=a\in\{8.0,5.0,4.0,3.0\} for d ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 } d\in\{5,10,20,30\} , respectively. Geometrically, the target has a sharp non-smooth peak at u = ( u k ) k = 1 d u=(u_{k})_{k=1}^{d} and decays exponentially in the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distance from it, producing diamond-shaped level sets with axis-aligned corners. As the dimension grows, its mass becomes increasingly concentrated in a small region of the domain, making accurate exploration and integration progressively more challenging.

sections.heading: Corner Peak Genz.
sections.text: The Corner Peak target is given by r ⁡ ( x ) = ( 1 + ∑ k = 1 d a k ​ x k ) − ( d + 1 ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d . r(x)=\left(1+\sum_{k=1}^{d}a_{k}x_{k}\right)^{-(d+1)},\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}. The density is largest at the corner x = 0 x=0 and decays as the weighted sum of the coordinates increases. For all coordinates we take a k = a ∈ { 0.50 , 0.25 , 0.10 , 0.08 } a_{k}=a\in\{0.50,0.25,0.10,0.08\} for d ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 } d\in\{5,10,20,30\} , respectively. Because the dominant probability mass is associated with a boundary corner rather than an interior mode, this benchmark probes the ability of the sampler to discover and represent boundary-concentrated distributions. The progressively smaller a k a_{k} values compensate for the increasing dimensionality and preserve a meaningful level of concentration across the dimensional sweep.

sections.heading: Discontinuous Genz.
sections.text: The Discontinuous Genz is defined by r ⁡ ( x ) = { exp ⁡ ( ∑ k = 1 d a k ​ x k ) , x k ≤ u k ​ ∀ k , 0 , otherwise . r(x)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{d}a_{k}x_{k}\right),&x_{k}\leq u_{k}\ \forall k,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} We set u k = 0.5 u_{k}=0.5 for all coordinates. The shared concentration parameter is a k = a ∈ { 5.0 , 4.0 , 3.0 , 3.0 } a_{k}=a\in\{5.0,4.0,3.0,3.0\} for d ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 } d\in\{5,10,20,30\} , respectively. This benchmark combines two distinct difficulties. First, the support is restricted to the subcube [ 0 , 0.5 ] d [0,0.5]^{d} , which introduces a sharp discontinuity at every boundary of the feasible region. Second, within the support the density increases exponentially with the coordinates, so that the mode is located at the upper corner ( 0.5 , … , 0.5 ) ⊤ (0.5,\ldots,0.5)^{\top} of the active region. Consequently, the sampler must simultaneously identify a discontinuous support restriction and concentrate probability near the boundary of that restricted support. In the implementation, we add a small positive correction of ε = 10 − 10 \varepsilon=10^{-10} to make a target reward strictly positive and then subtract ε ​ vol ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \varepsilon\vol(\mathcal{D}) in the final estimate.

sections.heading: Gaussian Peak Genz.
sections.text: The Gaussian Peak Genz is defined by r ( x ) = exp ( − ∑ k = 1 d a k 2 ( x k − u k ) 2 ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d . r(x)=\exp\left(-\sum_{k=1}^{d}a_{k}^{2}(x_{k}-u_{k})^{2}\right),\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}. We use u k = 0.5 u_{k}=0.5 for all coordinates and set a k = a ∈ { 8.0 , 5.0 , 4.0 , 3.0 } a_{k}=a\in\{8.0,5.0,4.0,3.0\} for d ∈ { 5 , 10 , 20 , 30 } d\in\{5,10,20,30\} , respectively. The resulting distribution is a sharply concentrated, smooth peak centred at the middle of the hypercube. Relative to the Continuous target, the Gaussian Peak is globally differentiable and has rapidly decaying tails away from its mode, making the pair useful for distinguishing the effect of nonsmoothness from that of concentration alone.

sections.heading: Product Peak Genz.
sections.text: The Product Peak Genz target is given by r ⁡ ( x ) = ∏ k = 1 d 1 a k − 2 + ( x k − u k ) 2 , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d . r(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{d}\frac{1}{a_{k}^{-2}+(x_{k}-u_{k})^{2}},\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}. We take u k = 0.5 u_{k}=0.5 in every coordinate. The shared coefficient a k = a a_{k}=a takes values 8.0 8.0 , 5.0 5.0 , 4.0 4.0 , and 4.0 4.0 for dimensions d = 5 d=5 , 10 10 , 20 20 , and 30 30 , respectively. The function factorizes across dimensions, but each factor exhibits a sharply localized peak around u k = 0.5 u_{k}=0.5 . In the implementation, we rescale r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) by the maximum reward for numerical stability and adjust the analytic normalizing constant accordingly.

sections.heading: GMM Cube.
sections.text: The GMM Cube target is a bounded multimodal distribution constructed by placing a mixture of five isotropic Gaussian components inside the unit hypercube. For a d d -dimensional target r ⁡ ( x ) = 1 5 ​ ∑ j = 1 5 𝒩 ⁡ ( x , μ j , σ 2 ​ I d ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d , r(x)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=1}^{5}\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_{j},\sigma^{2}I_{d}),\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}, with σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 . The component locations are sampled once from the interior region [ 0.01 , 0.99 ] d [0.01,0.99]^{d} , thereby ensuring all modes remain separated from the boundary. The target is subsequently restricted to the unit cube. This construction produces a genuinely multimodal bounded target in which the sampler must discover several well-separated regions of high probability rather than a single dominant mode. Because the Gaussian mixture is initially defined on the full Euclidean space and then restricted to the cube, its normalization constant is the probability that a draw from the unconstrained mixture falls inside [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} . This quantity is estimated in the implementation by Monte Carlo sampling from the unconstrained mixture. The target therefore tests both multimodal exploration and the ability to account for truncation by the bounded domain.

sections.heading: Stripe Cube.
sections.text: The Stripe Cube target is designed to concentrate probability near the boundary of the unit hypercube while retaining a small positive density throughout its interior. For a point x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d x\in[0,1]^{d} , define the distance to the closest boundary face by δ ⁡ ( x ) = min i ⁡ { x i , 1 − x i } \delta(x)=\min_{i}\{x_{i},1-x_{i}\} . We map this distance to a normalized boundary score s ⁡ ( x ) = 1 − 2 ​ δ ​ ( x ) s(x)=1-2\delta(x) , which equals zero at the centre of the cube and one on the boundary. The target density is then r ⁡ ( x ) = α + ( β − α ) ​ s γ ​ ( x ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d , r(x)=\alpha+(\beta-\alpha)s^{\gamma}(x),\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}, where α = 10 − 10 , β = 1 \alpha=10^{-10},\beta=1 and γ = 8 \gamma=8 . Hence the density rises steeply as a point approaches any boundary face, producing a set of high-probability boundary ”stripes” around the cube while retaining a numerically nonzero floor in its interior. Whereas the Corner Peak benchmark concentrates mass near a single corner, Stripe Cube assigns high density collectively to all boundary faces. The resulting target therefore contains a large, geometrically thin high-density region whose total structure becomes increasingly complex with dimension. The normalization constant is available analytically Z = α + ( β − α ) ​ d d + γ . Z=\alpha+\left(\beta-\alpha\right)\frac{d}{d+\gamma}.

sections.heading: Funnel Cube.
sections.text: The Funnel Cube target is a bounded analogue of the classical funnel distribution and is designed to test adaptation to strongly varying conditional scales. The first coordinate follows a Gaussian density, x 1 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0.6 , 0.22 2 ) , x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0.6,0.22^{2}), restricted to the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Conditional on x 1 x_{1} , the remaining d − 1 d-1 coordinates are independent Gaussian variables centered at 0.5 0.5 with a standard deviation that changes exponentially across the first coordinate: log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( x 1 ) = log ⁡ σ min + x 1 ​ ( log ⁡ σ max − log ⁡ σ min ) , \log\sigma(x_{1})=\log\sigma_{\mathrm{min}}+x_{1}\left(\log\sigma_{\mathrm{max}}-\log\sigma_{\mathrm{min}}\right), where σ min = 0.02 \sigma_{\mathrm{min}}=0.02 and σ max = 0.30 \sigma_{\mathrm{max}}=0.30 . The target density can therefore be written as r ⁡ ( x ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( x 1 , 0.6 , 0.22 2 ) ​ ∏ k = 2 d 𝒩 ⁡ ( x k , 0.5 , σ 2 ​ ( x 1 ) ) , x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d . r(x)=\mathcal{N}(x_{1};0.6,0.22^{2})\prod_{k=2}^{d}\mathcal{N}\!\left(x_{k};0.5,\sigma^{2}(x_{1})\right),\qquad x\in[0,1]^{d}. The defining difficulty of this benchmark is the strong dependence of the conditional width on x 1 x_{1} . Samples associated with one region of the first coordinate lie in a very narrow tube around 0.5 0.5 , whereas samples associated with another region can occupy a considerably wider cross-section. The target therefore tests whether a learned sampler can represent pronounced heteroscedasticity rather than simply locating isolated modes. Its normalization constant is computed by reducing the d d -dimensional integral to a one-dimensional numerical integration over x 1 x_{1} , where the probability that every remaining coordinate lies in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] is evaluated analytically.

sections.heading: Asian option.
sections.text: We consider Asian option pricing as an application-oriented high-dimensional benchmark with a nonsmooth payoff and a strong temporal dependence structure, following the standard construction L’Ecuyer (2009) . The implementation is based on a discretised Black–Scholes asset path. A point x = ( x 1 , … , x d ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in[0,1]^{d} is first transformed into independent standard-normal shocks through the inverse Gaussian cumulative distribution function, ϵ i = Φ − 1 ​ ( x i ) \epsilon_{i}=\Phi^{-1}(x_{i}) . For monitoring times 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t d = T 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{d}=T , the Brownian path is then constructed as W t j = ∑ i = 1 j t i − t i − 1 ​ ϵ i , W_{t_{j}}=\sum_{i=1}^{j}\sqrt{t_{i}-t_{i-1}}\,\epsilon_{i}, and the corresponding asset price at time t j t_{j} is S t j = S 0 ​ exp ⁡ [ ( r − 1 2 ​ σ 2 ) ​ t j + σ ​ W t j ] . S_{t_{j}}=S_{0}\exp\left[\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\right)t_{j}+\sigma W_{t_{j}}\right]. The default parameters are S 0 = 100 S_{0}=100 , r = log ⁡ ( 1.09 ) r=\log(1.09) , σ = 0.2 \sigma=0.2 , and T = 120 365 T=\frac{120}{365} . The reward is given by the discounted arithmetic-average call payoff r ⁡ ( x ) = e − r ​ T ​ max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 d ​ ∑ i = 1 d S t i − K ) , r(x)=e^{-rT}\max(0,\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}S_{t_{i}}-K), where K K is the strike price. The arithmetic average couples the payoff to the entire simulated trajectory, while the positive-part operator introduces a nonsmooth boundary and makes the reward exactly zero over a substantial portion of the input domain. We consider two principal configurations from Example 3 ( L’Ecuyer, 2009 ) . The easy problem has dimension d = 10 d=10 , uses a starting monitoring period of 111 111 days, a strike of K = 90 K=90 , and has a ground-truth option value Z = 13.008 Z=13.008 . The hard problem increases the dimension to d = 120 d=120 , starts monitoring at period 1 1 , retains the strike K = 90 K=90 , and has Z = 11.207 Z=11.207 . The difference between the two settings therefore changes both the number of Gaussian increments used to represent the asset path and the portion of the maturity interval entering the arithmetic average. The hard configuration consequently presents a substantially higher-dimensional integration problem with a longer temporal dependence structure, providing a stringent test of the sampler’s scalability. As for the Genz Discontinuous benchmark, we add a small constant ε = 10 − 10 \varepsilon=10^{-10} to the reward to make it strictly positive. We remove this artificial contribution from the final integral estimate by subtracting ε ​ vol ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \varepsilon\vol(\mathcal{D}) .

sections.heading: Digits.
sections.text: We adapt the Digits benchmark from Blessing et al. (2024) , where the target is a NICE normalizing-flow density ( Dinh et al., 2014 ) trained on downsampled 14 × 14 14\times 14 MNIST images. The original target is a normalized continuous density p NICE p_{\mathrm{NICE}} on ℝ 196 \mathbb{R}^{196} . To obtain a bounded-domain integration problem, we apply the coordinate-wise logit transformation and define the cube target by the corresponding change of variables, r ⁡ ( x ) = p NICE ​ ( logit ⁡ ( x ) ) ​ ∏ j = 1 196 1 x j ​ ( 1 − x j ) . r(x)=p_{\mathrm{NICE}}(\operatorname{logit}(x))\prod_{j=1}^{196}\frac{1}{x_{j}(1-x_{j})}. This transformation preserves the normalizing constant, so Z = 1 Z=1 . Samples generated on the cube can be mapped back through the logit transformation and reshaped into 14 × 14 14\times 14 grayscale images. Beyond integration, this benchmark provides a challenging high-dimensional sampling task with complex learned structure, allowing us to test whether RDS can recover meaningful samples from the target distribution itself.

sections.heading: Elliptic Two-Loop.
sections.text: The Elliptic Two-Loop target is a Feynman-parameter integral arising in collider phenomenology. sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We compare methods across different budgets corresponding to the number of points used for the integral estimation. For neural network-based methods, namely PIS, ZüNIS and RDS, for a fixed number of points used for evaluation, the same number of points is used for training. For these methods we use a batch size of 512 512 in all experiments. We report the mean absolute error | Z ^ − Z | |\widehat{Z}-Z| over independent runs as a function of the number of points. For all experiments we present mean and std of the error across 3 random seeds.

sections.heading: Quasi-Monte Carlo.
sections.text: As a non-adaptive baseline, we use randomized quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) with scrambled Sobol sequences L’Ecuyer (2009) . For a budget N = 2 m N=2^{m} , we generate N N points x ( 1 ) , … , x ( N ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(N)}\in[0,1]^{d} from a scrambled Sobol sequence and estimate Z ^ QMC = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N r ⁡ ( x ( i ) ) . \widehat{Z}_{\mathrm{QMC}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r(x^{(i)}). (85) Independent random scramblings are used across runs. Using powers of two preserves the digital-net structure of the Sobol construction. QMC does not involve any optimization, and its target-evaluation budget is exactly N N . We use SciPy implementation Virtanen et al. (2020) .

sections.heading: Fast Fourier Bayesian Quadrature.
sections.text: We use the public implementation of Fast Fourier Bayesian Quadrature (FFBQ) by Warren & Ramos (2024) . FFBQ approximates the integrand with a Gaussian process and computes the resulting Bayesian-quadrature estimate using scalable convolution operators. In our experiments, we fit a low-rank GP with an RBF kernel using 5,000 5{,}000 uniformly sampled training points and use an independent set of 5,000 5{,}000 points for quadrature evaluation. We employ the sparse QMC convolution operator provided by the authors. Low-rank GP was chosen, because of the scalability issues with dimension of FFBQ. The GP training and evaluation sets are fixed across experiments, while we vary the number N N of QMC samples used to approximate the final convolution integral.

sections.heading: Path Integral Sampler.
sections.text: We include the Path Integral Sampler (PIS) ( Zhang & Chen, 2022 ) , an on-policy diffusion sampler derived from a stochastic-control formulation of sampling. To apply PIS on the bounded domain, we instead use a change of variables between ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} and [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} . Specifically, for z ∈ ℝ d z\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , we set x = σ ⁡ ( z ) x=\sigma(z) , where σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is a sigmoid function. Accordingly, PIS is trained on the transformed reward r ~ ​ ( z ) = r ⁡ ( σ ⁡ ( z ) ) ​ | det J σ ​ ( z ) | , \widetilde{r}(z)=r\!\left(\sigma(z)\right)\left|\det J_{\sigma}(z)\right|, which preserves the original integral by the change-of-variables formula. The control is parameterized by an MLP with four hidden layers of width 256 256 . We train PIS with Adam using a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Each diffusion trajectory is discretized using 64 64 time steps. The control is trained using the standard path-space objective consisting of the accumulated quadratic control cost and the terminal target-density contribution. The resulting estimate of Z Z is obtained using the path-integral importance weights associated with the learned controlled process. For PIS, we used a public implementation from Blessing et al. (2024) .

sections.heading: ZüNIS.
sections.text: We use the public implementation of ZüNIS ( Deutschmann & Götz, 2024 ) . The proposal is parameterized by a bounded piecewise-quadratic coupling flow with 8 8 coupling layers, 10 10 bins per scalar transformation, and conditioner networks with two hidden layers of width 256 256 . We optimize the proposal with the reverse-KL objective using Adam with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and global gradient-norm clipping at 1 1 . The first batch is sampled uniformly from the cube, while all subsequent batches are drawn from the current flow proposal. Each evaluated survey batch is used for a single optimization update. sections.heading: RDS-RP and RDS-RF.
sections.text: Both variants use the same reflected diffusion and differ only in the gradient estimator used for training. We employ the Langevin parameterization of the drift, following Zhang & Chen (2022) and Blessing et al. (2024) : s θ ​ ( x , t ) = clip ⁡ ( a θ ​ ( x , t ) + b θ ​ ( t ) ⊙ clip ⁡ ( ∇ x ​ log ​ r ​ ( x ) , − 10 2 , 10 2 ) , − 10 4 , 10 4 ) , s_{\theta}(x,t)=\operatorname{clip}\left(a_{\theta}(x,t)+b_{\theta}(t)\odot\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\nabla_{x}\log r(x),-10^{2},10^{2}\bigr),-10^{4},10^{4}\right), (87) where a θ ​ ( x , t ) a_{\theta}(x,t) is a time-conditioned neural network, b θ ​ ( t ) ∈ ℝ d b_{\theta}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a learned time-dependent coordinate-wise scaling function, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. This parameterization incorporates the target score directly into the drift while allowing the neural network to learn a flexible time-dependent correction. For targets with zero-valued regions we do not incorporate ∇ x ​ log ​ r ​ ( x ) \nabla_{x}\log r(x) to the parameterization. The score network is parameterized by a 4 4 -layer MLP with hidden width 256 256 . We use σ 0 = 10 − 3 \sigma_{0}=10^{-3} and σ 1 = 1 \sigma_{1}=1 , and discretize the diffusion into 64 64 reflected steps for integration tasks. Both models are trained on-policy with Adam using the same optimization hyperparameters and global gradient-norm clipping at 1 1 . For RDS-RP, gradients are propagated through the simulated trajectory using the reparameterized Gaussian increments and the coordinate-wise reflection map. Since reflection on the cube is piecewise linear, it is differentiable almost everywhere and can be handled directly by automatic differentiation. RDS-RF instead uses the score-function estimator described in Section 3.4 . The sampled states are treated as stop-gradient quantities, while the dependence on the proposal parameters is captured through the scores of the Gaussian transitions and their corresponding cost-to-go terms. Thus, RDS-RP and RDS-RF use the same proposal family, discretization, and training objective, providing a direct comparison between pathwise and score-function optimization. Our implementations are based upon the published codebase of Blessing et al. (2024) .

sections.heading: Digits experiments.
sections.text: For the Digits benchmark, we use the PIS architecture and remaining training hyperparameters following Blessing et al. (2024) . Both PIS and RDS are discretized using 128 128 diffusion steps and trained with Adam using a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , batch size of 2048 2048 and 40,000 40,000 iterations.
